## Mexico City — a City of Contrasts!

Mexico City, the world's largest city and one of the most densely populated places on the planet, lies in a picturesque valley surrounded by mountains. It was built on the site of a settlement of the legendary Aztec people, whose wealth and cruelty live on in numerous legends. Mexico City is a metropolis. It is a city of contrasts, where ultra-modern skyscrapers stand alongside ancient pyramids, and poor neighborhoods that can be dangerous for tourists coexist with magnificent palaces. It is also an “open-air museum,” preserving more than 1,400 monuments and historical relics.

The city and its surroundings contain 10 archaeological zones, 8 universities, several academies, more than 80 museums, theaters, concert halls, and exhibition venues. The National Palace is particularly interesting: paintings by the renowned artist Diego Rivera trace the country's history. Visit Frida's house museum, where Trotsky lived at the beginning of his exile.

## Excursions in Mexico City and to the Ruins of Teotihuacan

Located 50 km northeast of the capital, Teotihuacan means “the place where gods are born.” It is a sacred complex for many Indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica. Ancient Teotihuacan is one of Mexico's most visited archaeological sites. The date of its first settlements and the reasons its inhabitants abandoned the city remain unknown. These “stone treasures of history,” assembled from enormous blocks, follow a strict but mysterious system. The complex is striking in scale: the Pyramid of the Sun is the third largest pyramid in the world.

## Tours Around Mexico City!

Just 50 km from Mexico City lie the impressive ruins of Teotihuacan. You will see the Pyramid of the Dead, the Temple of Quetzalcoatl, and many other monuments of an unknown civilization that existed here 1,000 years before the Aztecs. This was the center of an empire whose borders reached El Salvador. Not far north of the city, you can enjoy views of the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl and descend to the volcanic lakes of the snowy Toluca Valley. Be sure to visit the area near the city where millions of colorful monarch butterflies migrate to spend the winter.

The Melchior Islands are a group of small islands in Dallmann Bay, part of the Palmer Archipelago off the Antarctic Peninsula. They lie between the larger islands of Brabant and Anvers. Low snow-covered shores, dark rocky outcrops, and channels between the islands create a landscape quite different from the high mountains of the neighboring islands.

The group includes Lambda, Gamma, Eta, and Omega islands, as well as smaller islets. The Sound separates its eastern and western sections. The name is associated with French Vice Admiral Jules-Bernard-François Melchior and Jean-Baptiste Charcot's expedition explorations in the early 20th century. On an expedition itinerary, you may explore the archipelago from the ship or by boat; sea and ice conditions determine which outings are possible.

Mendoza lies in western Argentina at the foot of the Andes. A city itinerary can combine Plaza Independencia, Plaza España, the administrative center, and the large San Martín Park.

For a gastronomic trip, the vineyards and wineries take center stage. The Ruta de los Vinos lets you spend one day or several days visiting the region's estates and discovering local wines.

Mendoza combines well with Buenos Aires and other destinations in western Argentina, with enough time set aside for wineries and trips into the Andes.

Mérida's attractions include the historic La Parroquia neighborhood, the church on Rangel del Llano Square, the university, the Floral Clock, and the colorful Mercado Principal de Mérida street market. There are numerous churches and chapels in the city and its surroundings.

In the surrounding area you can see the lake known as “Black Lagoon.” Near the city are Condor Park, Sierra Nevada National Park, and the national observatory.

Mérida is a city on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. Its historic center features squares, colonial architecture, and streets lined with low buildings painted in warm, bright colors. Walking here adds contemporary city life and Yucatecan cuisine to an itinerary focused on the region's archaeological sites.

On trips through Yucatán, Mérida is often an overnight stop between visits to Uxmal and Chichén Itzá. Such a stop leaves time to enjoy the city center in the evening and explore at an unhurried pace after sightseeing transfers. This is Mérida in Mexico; when selecting routes and reference materials, the country matters because a city with the same name also exists in Venezuela.
